To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the more the victim is seen as deserving of suffering, the more the observers will derogate the victim and the more they will derogate the perpetrator.

(1) the more severe the suffering, the more likely it is that the victim will be derogated, and (2) when the victim is perceived as being a good person, he will be sympathetically treated regardless of the degree of his suffering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why people sometimes respond with compassion and at other times with rejection when faced with the suffering of another.
the effects of characterological information about the victim on observers' reactions to undeserved suffering.
the question of whether the suffering of innocent victims will elicit compassion or rejection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the degree of suffering is the most influential factor in determining whether the victim will be derogated or not.
the degree of suffering of the victim is a major factor in determining the observers' response.

the present study has demonstrated that observers are capable of responding in a sympathetic fashion to undeserved suffering, even when the victim is viewed unfavorably, provided the victim is viewed as suffering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the degree to which a victim is derogated is a function of the degree of suffering, the characterological information about the victim, and the interaction of these variables.
observers' responses to an innocent victim are a function of the degree of suffering and the victim's characterological qualities.
observers do not automatically derogate innocent victims.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the way people react to the suffering of others is not a function of the suffering per se, but of the context in which the suffering occurs, particularly the victim's character and the observer's relationship to the victim.
the context matters, and that context includes the character of the person suffering.
we need to be careful not to judge people based on their suffering alone.
